young.html: When Charles Darwin was 22, he sailed around the world on a ship called the Beagle. For five years he collected beetles, birds, fossils and plants. On the Galápagos Islands he noticed that each island had its own kinds of finches and tortoises, a little different from the next island's.
Back home in England he wondered why. After twenty years of thinking and experimenting, he wrote On the Origin of Species (1859). His big idea, natural selection, goes like this:

items: Living things are all a little different, even brothers and sisters.
Many of those differences are passed on to the young.
More young are born than can possibly survive.
The ones whose differences help them live are more likely to grow up and have young of their own.
Over a very long time, these small changes add up, and new kinds of living things appear.

Darwin's own nature table: he loved simple experiments, like counting seedlings in a patch of ground he had cleared, or floating seeds in salt water to see if they could cross the sea. You can try both.

full.html: Charles Darwin (1809–1882), grandson of the physician-poet Erasmus Darwin and of the potter Josiah Wedgwood, studied medicine at Edinburgh and then trained for the church at Cambridge, where he fell in love with natural history. From 1831 to 1836 he sailed as naturalist on HMS Beagle, reading Charles Lyell's Principles of Geology on the way. In 1838 he read Thomas Malthus on population and saw how selection could work. He wrote sketches of his theory in 1842 and 1844 but held back for years, gathering evidence. In 1858 Alfred Russel Wallace, working in the Malay islands, sent him an essay with the same idea; their papers were presented together that July, and Darwin hurried out the Origin, published November 24, 1859.

Darwin called the book "one long argument." It starts with what breeders of pigeons, dogs and crops already knew: by choosing which animals have young, they change a breed a great deal in a few generations. Then comes the struggle for existence: every species produces far more young than can survive.

full.title: Darwin's doubling plants
full.q: Darwin imagined an annual plant making only two seeds a year, all of which grew. Starting from one plant, how many after 20 years?
full.a: About a million plants, so most seeds in nature must fail to grow up.

full.text: Can it, then, be thought improbable, seeing that variations useful to man have undoubtedly occurred, that other variations useful in some way to each being in the great and complex battle of life, should sometimes occur in the course of thousands of generations? ... This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection.

full.html: Darwin piles up evidence: the fossil record, the way species are spread across the globe (island species resemble those of the nearest mainland), the shared body plans of very different animals, and embryos. He also faces his "difficulties on theory" head-on: how could an organ as complex as the eye arise by small steps? Why are there gaps in the fossil record? He answers each in turn, and admits what he cannot yet explain.

Darwin's theory has two parts. Descent with modification: all living things are related, descended from common ancestors. Natural selection: the main way they change. Darwin saw life as a branching tree; the book's only illustration is a branching diagram.

full.text: There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.
full.author: Darwin
full.work: On the Origin of Species, closing sentence
full.note: From the second edition on, Darwin added "by the Creator" after "breathed."

full.html: Darwin did not know how inheritance works; his own guess was wrong. Gregor Mendel's experiments with peas (1866) were rediscovered in 1900, and in the 1930s and 1940s biologists joined genetics and natural selection in the "modern synthesis." DNA, fossils found since, and observed cases of evolution, such as bacteria becoming resistant to antibiotics, have confirmed descent with modification. Evolution by natural selection is the foundation of modern biology, though scientists still study how much other forces, such as chance drift, contribute.

The book also raised religious questions. Some readers saw it as a threat to faith; others, such as the American botanist Asa Gray, Darwin's friend, saw no conflict between evolution and belief in a Creator. Darwin himself described his views late in life as agnostic. Readers today still hold a range of views on how science and faith fit together.
Thinking individuals evolve. In natural selection no single animal changes its traits; the makeup of the population changes over generations.

items: Aristotle's biology, earlier on this ladder, had classified animals by fixed kinds; Darwin made the kinds themselves change.
Lucretius imagined creatures that failed to survive in a world of atoms, a distant ancestor of the idea.
Malthus and Adam Smith: ideas of population and competition from economics helped Darwin see nature's economy.
The Descent of Man, Darwin's next rung, applies the theory to human beings.
